blind_spots: No evidence quantifying how frequently false accusations occur versus genuine AI use, leaving prevalence unclear.
Little direct first-person testimony from writers (most writing evidence is mediated through journalism); the writer/author perspective is thinner than the visual-artist perspective.
No evidence on financial/income impact (lost clients, lost commissions) despite mention of client perception.
No evidence on platform or marketplace policy responses to false accusations.
Author-side perspective on whether to commission human artists from AI references (Nathan the Author tweet) raises an unresolved etiquette question with no resolution in evidence.
contradictions: Some artists demand reliable detection tools as a solution, while other evidence shows detection tools themselves misidentify human work as AI, undermining them as a remedy.
Many creators report fear of disclosing AI use, yet evidence also notes that many artists and writers do openly use AI in limited ways (idea generation, references, backgrounds).
Accusers admit 'AI-looking' traits are not reliable proof, yet style/vibe-based accusations continue to spread widely.
